name: AutoConstrain
tooltip: Generates options using AI technology to automatically dimension and constrain your sketch. Review the proposals and select the one that best suits your needs.

history.note: I couldn't compare this feature because Fusion refuses to run it on this account. AutoConstrain uses AI to propose constraints and dimensions for a sketch. Fusion's API has it as Sketch.autoConstrain with three result options, and only Option 3 can change geometry: it may snap small inaccuracies, such as a nearly-horizontal line. I wrote a case that draws a slightly skewed 40x30 quad, runs AutoConstrain with Option 3, then extrudes it 20 mm. Fusion stopped with 'RuntimeError: 3 : AutoConstrain is not available since user is restricted', so there is no answer key. Fox has no matching command either: sketch.constrain only adds one constraint you choose, and the 'Finish with AutoConstrain' menu item in crates/ui/src/menus.rs has no command behind it. If the probe ever runs, expect it to come back fox-missing. Cases: none.

name: AutoConstrain from datum
tooltip: Place a datum point to align the constraints and dimensions to, then AI technology automatically generates options with dimension and constraints added your sketch. Review the proposals and select the one that best suits your needs.

history.note: AutoConstrain from datum uses AI to add geometric constraints and dimensions to an existing sketch, relative to a datum point you pick. It leaves the geometry where it is, so volume, area, bounding box and face count can't show whether it worked, and no geometry case was built. Fusion's API can run it from a script (Sketch.createAutoConstrainInput, then autoConstrain, with datumPoint, dimensionStrategy, symmetricDimensionStrategy, interLoopDimensionStrategy, linearDiameterDimensionPreference and resultOption), but its result is a constraint state such as isFullyConstrained, not a solid. Fox has no auto-constrain command: the candidates drawing.datum and drawing.datum_target are GD&T drawing annotations, and sketch.constrain only adds one manual constraint at a time. Cases: none.

A fix would add a `sketch.auto_constrain {sketch, datum_point?, dimension_strategy?, symmetric?, result_option?}` command in crates/sketch, with the command registered in crates/engine. It would infer the constraints the geometry already satisfies (coincident, horizontal or vertical, parallel, perpendicular, tangent, equal, symmetric), then add dimensions measured from the datum point until the degrees of freedom reported by sketch.info reach 0, without moving the geometry. name: Concentric
tooltip: Constrains two or more arcs, circles, or ellipses to the same center point.

history.note: Tested the Concentric sketch constraint on a chain of three circles, an arc (half disc with line, radius dimension, centre on the line) made concentric with a construction circle, and a circle made concentric with an ellipse. Fox matches Fusion exactly for circles and arcs, but rejects concentric when one curve is an ellipse ("Concentric needs circles or arcs"), so the hole stays off-centre (centre of mass off by (-0.43,-0.26), 5 faces vs 4). probe.fix_hint: crates/sketch/src/lib.rs ~line 806: the check for ConstraintKind::Concentric uses `round()`, which only accepts circles and arcs, so it needs to accept CurveKind::Ellipse too. crates/sketch/src/solve.rs ~line 707: K::Concentric gets each centre from self.round(x, id), so it needs a centre lookup that also returns an ellipse's centre point. When the solver moves an ellipse's centre, its major-axis point should move with it (Fusion slides the ellipse across; it does not turn or resize it).

fix.summary:
Fusion's Concentric constraint accepts arcs, circles and ellipses. Fox rejected ellipses with "Concentric needs circles or arcs", so the hole in case 103 stayed off-centre.

What changed:
- **The check** (`crates/sketch/src/lib.rs`): Concentric now accepts ellipses and elliptical arcs. Radius and Diameter still accept only circles and arcs.
- **The solver** (`crates/sketch/src/solve.rs`): Concentric now finds each curve's centre with a new `centre()` lookup, which also returns an ellipse's centre point. An ellipse's major-axis point now moves with its centre when it is "free": no constraint names it, no other curve uses it, and neither point is fixed or held. The solver handles this by solving twice. The first pass ties the free major-axis point to the centre, so the ellipse slides across without turning or resizing, as it does in Fusion. The second pass frees every point so the solve report still gives the right degrees of freedom and free points. If the first pass can't satisfy the constraints, Fox falls back to the all-free solve. A new unit test covers sliding an ellipse onto a circle, a constrained major-axis end, moving a circle onto a fixed ellipse, and rejecting a line.
- **Profiles** (`crates/sketch/src/profile.rs`): a loop made only of same-direction arcs of one ellipse that together cover the whole ellipse becomes a single closed ellipse edge. The extruded plate then has 4 faces, matching Fusion, instead of 5.

New reference cases 101-concentric-circle-chain, 102-concentric-arc-to-circle and 103-concentric-circle-to-ellipse all pass and are in baseline.txt. 101 also survives the edit check and is in edit-baseline.txt; the test reported nothing else to add there.

Checks: `cargo test -p fox-engine --test reference_parts` passes with no regressions, the fox-sketch unit tests pass (51), and `cargo fmt` and `cargo clippy -p fox-sketch --all-targets -D warnings` are clean.

One failure outside this change: in the full `cargo test -p fox-engine` run, `fuzz_features::fuzz_found_bugs` fails (seed 1022 produces an invalid solid). It fails the same way with main's sketch crate, so this change didn't cause it.

name: Curvature
tooltip: Constrains two or more objects to create a smooth, continuous curvature between them (G2 continuity).

history.note: I tested Fusion's Curvature (G2) constraint, which the API calls addSmooth, between a fitted spline and a fixed arc or line. In every case all of the spline's fit points were fixed, so only the spline's end shape could change. Fusion solved all three cases and built the solids. Fox's `sketch.constrain` with type curvature exists but rejects all three with "that constraint conflicts with the others (or over-constrains the sketch)", so the sketch is extruded without the constraint. Fox only satisfies G2 if it is allowed to move the fit points. Separately, Fox gives one face per Bézier piece of the spline, so it reports 9 faces where Fusion has 7. Cases: 104-spline-arc-curvature, 105-spline-line-curvature, 106-spline-arc-same-turn-curvature.

probe.summary: I tested Fusion's Curvature (G2) constraint, which the API calls addSmooth, between a fitted spline and a fixed arc or line. In every case all of the spline's fit points were fixed, so only the spline's end shape could change. Fusion solved all three cases and built the solids. Fox's `sketch.constrain` with type curvature exists but rejects all three with "that constraint conflicts with the others (or over-constrains the sketch)", so the sketch is extruded without the constraint. Fox only satisfies G2 if it is allowed to move the fit points. Separately, Fox gives one face per Bézier piece of the spline, so it reports 9 faces where Fusion has 7.
probe.fix_hint: The feature is `sketch.constrain {type: curvature|smooth|g2}` (crates/engine/src/commands.rs ~2510), not the `sketch.blend` candidate: that is the separate Blend Curve tool. The gap is the spline's freedom at the joint. When a Tangent or Curvature constraint is added, `Sketch::add_spline_handle` (crates/sketch/src/freeform.rs ~1150, called from lib.rs `add_constraint`) gives `CurveKind::Spline` only a tangent handle: `end_handle`/`start_handle`, the inner control point of the end piece. The curvature at the end also depends on the end piece's other inner control point (b1), and that comes from interpolating the fit points. So with the fit points fixed, the residual `(ka + kb)` in solve.rs `smooth()` usually can't reach zero, the solve fails, and commands.rs reports a conflict. Fusion turns on both a tangent handle and a curvature handle on a fitted spline, which lets it meet G2 while the fit points stay put. A fix would add a curvature degree of freedom at the constrained end. Options are a second handle point that drives b1 of the end piece, or a scalar curvature/tangent-length parameter. `kind_beziers`/`end_frame` would need to honour it and the solver would need to treat it as a free variable. Secondary: Fox splits a fitted spline into several Bézier faces when extruded (9 faces vs Fusion's 7), which affects face counts. Also, tools/fusion-bridge/FoxBridge/recipe_runner.py now names each fitted-spline fit point `<id>.fit<i>`, so recipes can fix them.

name: Fix/UnFix
tooltip: Locks the size and location of a point or object.

So a -90° arc from (20,0) to (0,-20) came out as the complementary 270° arc, with 3× the volume and a mirrored bounding box (case 157).

Changes:
- **`sketch.arc` command** (`crates/engine/src/commands.rs`):
  - New form `{center, start, sweep: angle}` takes a signed sweep as a number in degrees or an expression; negative means clockwise.
  - The existing `{center, start, end}` form takes an optional `clockwise: bool`.
  - It refuses a sweep of 0 or 360°, and a call that gives both `end` and `sweep`.
  - The command help lists the new options.
- **`Sketch::add_arc_center_dir`** (`crates/sketch/src/build.rs`): new method. Arcs are stored counter-clockwise, so it stores a clockwise arc with its ends swapped; the start point stays the shared one. `add_arc_center` now calls it with counter-clockwise, so existing callers are unchanged.
- **UI Center Point Arc tool** (`crates/ui/src/viewport.rs`): once the start is placed, it tracks how far the cursor has wound around the centre, either way, and previews that arc instead of a full circle. On the third click it sends `clockwise` when the cursor wound clockwise. This UI part isn't covered by any test and I didn't try it in the running app.
- **Case 157 script**: `part.jsonl` now uses `"sweep": -90`, as in the recipe (`sweep_deg: -90`), instead of an end point.
- **Baseline**: cases 155–157 added to `baseline.txt`. The test didn't ask for any `edit-baseline.txt` entries.
- **New unit test** `tests_sketch::centre_arc_sweeps_clockwise`: checks a quarter sector made with `sweep: -90` and with `clockwise: true`, a 270° pac-man made with `sweep: "270 deg"`, and the three refused inputs.

Testing:
- `cargo test -p fox-engine --test reference_parts` passes, with no regressions.
- The `fox-engine` lib tests (including the new test) and the `fox-sketch` tests pass.
- `cargo test -p fox-engine --test fuzz_features fuzz_found_bugs` fails, but it fails the same way on the parent commit, and its script doesn't use arcs.
- `cargo fmt` is done.
- `cargo clippy -p fox-sketch -p fox-engine -p fox-ui --all-targets -D warnings` is clean only with `-A clippy::chunks_exact_to_as_chunks`. That lint comes from the local clippy 0.1.99, newer than CI's pinned 1.97, and it fires in crates this change doesn't touch (render-gl, trace, exchange).

- **Direction:** the cross product of (start − centre) and (end − centre) now picks the direction. The slot goes counter-clockwise only when that sweep is 180° or less; otherwise it is built clockwise.
- **New option:** a `ccw` bool forces either direction, so slots over 180° can still be scripted. The command's help text is updated.
- **Radius:** the start point sets the radius, and the end point is projected onto that radius so it only sets the direction. This matches Fusion and keeps the radius right when the arc is swapped to run clockwise.

The degree also has to reach the rendering/bbox code and the STEP/DXF export in crates/engine/src/files.rs (about lines 507 and 575), which turns the curve back into control points. 2) Topology: a multi-span control spline should make one edge and one face, not one per Bezier span. probe.summary: Fusion's Control Point Spline (5D) builds a degree-5 spline from the control points. Fox's sketch.control_spline only builds cubics: it has no degree option, so `"degree": 5` is ignored. In both cases the profile is a degree-5 control-point spline closed with a line along X, extruded 10 mm. Fusion makes one smooth spline face (4 faces in total). Fox makes a cubic split into Bezier pieces, with 6 faces for the 6-point case and 9 for the 9-point case. Fox's volume is 13% too high with 6 points and 1.2% too low with 9; the area and bounding-box height also differ.
probe.fix_hint:
The gap is in four places:
- crates/sketch/src/lib.rs: CurveKind::ControlSpline { points } has no degree, and bspline_beziers() hard-codes p = 3. It splits the curve into cubic Bezier pieces, so each span becomes its own face.
- crates/engine/src/commands.rs (~line 2356, "sketch.control_spline"): never reads a degree.
- Command help (commands.rs:106): has no degree parameter.
- crates/engine/src/files.rs:507-517: the import path needs to keep the degree too.

A fix needs four parts:
1. Add a `degree` field (default 3, serde default) to ControlSpline and accept `degree: 3|5` in sketch.control_spline.
2. Evaluate a clamped uniform B-spline of that degree. If there are too few points, use degree = min(degree, n-1).
3. Hand the face/edge builder a single B-spline edge (Geom2d/Geom_BSplineCurve with clamped uniform knots), not one edge per Bezier span. Fusion gives the whole spline one face even when it is cubic with interior knots.
4. Update the sketch tessellation, profile and DXF/export paths that call bspline_beziers.

The face-count gap (Fox 6 or 9 faces vs Fusion 4) probably affects degree-3 control splines too. Check the drawcvmspline3d probe.

Fusion's Control Point Spline (5D) builds a degree-5 clamped uniform B-spline, and the whole spline becomes one face when extruded. Fox ignored `degree` and always built a cubic. Its kernel also turned every Bezier span into its own edge, giving 6 or 9 faces where Fusion has 4.

  - Above degree 3 it splits the curve into its Bezier spans, then fits each span with 16 cubic pieces. Each piece matches the true curve's points and first derivatives at its ends. A unit test checks this against de Boor's algorithm.

- **Command (`sketch.control_spline`):** accepts `degree` from 1 to 9 (default 3), and the command help says so.
- **Kernel (`kernel.cpp`):** where consecutive cubic segments in a profile or path meet with the same first derivative, they are joined into one cubic B-spline edge. Knots are removed where possible. A spline is now one edge and one side face, as in Fusion.
- **DXF import and export:** both keep the degree.

history.note: I tested Fit Point Spline (`sketch.spline` in Fox) with four extruded profiles: a 3-point arch, a 5-point wave, unevenly spaced fit points, and a closed spline. All four built in both apps, and all four came out a different shape in Fox. Volume differs by 4.5% to 19%, the bounding box is off by up to 3.3 mm, and Fusion makes one face per spline where Fox makes one per segment. Fox draws the curve through the fit points a different way from Fusion, can't make a smooth closed spline, and never bulges past the end points the way Fusion does in the uneven case (x from -0.88 to 40.88). probe.summary: I tested Fit Point Spline (`sketch.spline` in Fox) with four extruded profiles: a 3-point arch, a 5-point wave, unevenly spaced fit points, and a closed spline. All four built in both apps, and all four came out a different shape in Fox. Volume differs by 4.5% to 19%, the bounding box is off by up to 3.3 mm, and Fusion makes one face per spline where Fox makes one per segment. Fox draws the curve through the fit points a different way from Fusion, can't make a smooth closed spline, and never bulges past the end points the way Fusion does in the uneven case (x from -0.88 to 40.88).
probe.fix_hint:
The gap is in crates/sketch/src/lib.rs. `spline_beziers()`, which `kind_beziers()` uses for `CurveKind::Spline`, builds a chain of separate cubic Béziers: Catmull-Rom tangents between points and half-chord tangents at the ends. Every piece becomes its own edge and face, and the shape isn't Fusion's. Fusion's fitted spline, read through `NurbsCurve3D.getData()`, is a single non-periodic degree-5 NURBS. It is flagged rational, but the weights weren't read; the evenly spaced x control points of the arch look consistent with all weights being 1. Its knots are clamped and evenly spaced, with about 5 spans per fit-point gap: the 3-point curve has 10 inner spans and 15 control points, the 4-point curve 15 spans and 20 control points. It looks like a smooth (minimum-energy) fit through the points. The uneven case bulges past the end points (x -0.88 to 40.88), which Fox's half-chord end tangents can't do.

A fix needs to:
(1) build Spline curves as one B-spline edge, so a spline gives one face, not one per Bézier piece. Look at how `kind_beziers` feeds the kernel profile and edge code.
(2) match Fusion's curve through the points: fit a quintic B-spline through the fit points that bends as little as possible, check it against the control points and knots Fusion gives (reproduce them with `sketchFittedSplines.add` plus `geometry.getData()`), then use those control points.
(3) support closed fit point splines, a periodic curve with no corner at the start point. Today, repeating the first point in `sketch.spline` leaves a corner there (and the rebuilt-spline code in fitspline.rs has no closed case). Fusion sets `isClosed` (a periodic spline); Fox needs a `closed` flag on `sketch.spline` or must detect when the first and last points are the same.

To support the closed case I extended recipe_runner.py's `fitted_spline` with `"closed": true`, which sets `isClosed`, and added a None check after `sketchFittedSplines.add`.

With the anchors adjusted, the three straight-line cases give the same face count and bounding box, but Fox's text is about 0.144% smaller than Fusion's, so volume is off by 0.29% and area by 0.2% (the limit is 0.1%). probe.fix_hint:
1) Height scale. In crates/sketch/src/text.rs, outline() sets k = height / cap, where cap is the font's OS/2 capital height (1467 units in Arial). Fusion gives the capital H a top of 1.00076 × height in Arial, Calibri and Courier New, and 0.97839 × height in Times New Roman. In Arial that is height / 1464.9 units, so Fox comes out about 0.144% small. One fix is to scale from the measured 'H' glyph height × 1.00076, which matches Arial, Calibri and Courier New. Times New Roman doesn't fit that rule, so check it before committing to it.
2) Text along a path. sketch.text has nothing like Fusion's setAsAlongPath (path curve, above/below, alignment, character spacing) or setAsFitOnPath. It needs a path parameter that lays the glyphs out along the curve.
3) Extrude default. When extrude is given no profiles, it takes every closed region in the sketch, including the glyph counters (the inside of O, A and so on). Fusion's extrude of a text object leaves the counters out. The extrude profile selection in crates/engine needs to treat text as its glyph regions only.
4) Placement conventions, for reference: Fusion puts the text's ink box at the frame corner (no left side bearing) and turns the text about the frame's centre. Fox anchors the pen origin and turns about the anchor. The test scripts adjust `at` for this.
5) Fusion options Fox lacks: horizontal and vertical alignment in the frame, character spacing, bold/italic text style, and horizontal or vertical flip.

For G2, Fox also gives 8 or 9 faces where Fusion gives 6 or 7, so Fox splits the blend into several faces where Fusion keeps it as one.

The fix goes in crates/sketch/src/freeform.rs, in Sketch::blend.

What Fox builds now:
- G1: a cubic Bezier with handles of chord/3.
- G2: a 6-point cubic B-spline with h = chord/5, which ends up as several faces after extrusion.

What Fusion builds:
- A single SketchFittedSpline through just the two end points, with Tangent (G1) or Smooth (G2) constraints.
- Its geometry is one degree-5 NURBS with 10 control points and knots [0x6, .2, .4, .6, .8, 1x6]. It is one edge, so it makes one face.
- The end tangents are much longer than Fox's. In the line U-turn (chord 20), the first control point sits 1.599 from the end for G1, giving a derivative of about 40 (twice the chord). For G2 it sits 1.728 from the end, with the next one at 5.184 along the tangent. In the arc case the ratios differ, so the length is not a fixed multiple of the chord; it looks like a fairness/energy-minimising fit.

The exact control points for all four cases are in parity/probes/blendg1curvesketchcmd/fusion-blend-nurbs.md.

Suggested fix:
- Build the blend as one degree-5 spline with that knot vector.
- Fit the end tangent and curvature lengths to the recorded Fusion data, or make it a 2-point fitted spline whose end handles are solved the way Fusion does.
- Keep it one edge so the extrusion gives one face.

Also, Fox's sketch.blend defaults to continuity g2 while Fusion's API defaults to G1 (isCurvatureContinuity=false).

I also added a 'blend' sketch entity (curves, near, continuity) to tools/fusion-bridge/FoxBridge/recipe_runner.py.

The gap is in Sketch::chamfer in crates/sketch/src/edit.rs (around line 323), which only accepts two lines whose endpoints coincide. To match Fusion it should work for any two non-parallel lines:
1. Find the intersection P of the two infinite lines.
2. On each line, keep the end farther from P (or a keep/near point, if one is given as in Fusion's API).
3. Place the chamfer points at P + d·unit(kept_end − P) along each line.
4. Move each line's other end to its chamfer point. This extends a line that stops short (apparent intersection) or trims one that overshoots (crossing).
5. Add the chamfer line between the two points.

- spline through (0,0), (10,8), (20,10), (30,18)
- line (0,0)-(30,0)
- line (30,-5)-(30,25)

The gap is in crates/model/src/assembly.rs, joint_transform. Its line `let mate = if flip { IDENTITY } else { from_rotation_x(PI) }` gives the reverse of Fusion's Joint. Fusion's default is the identity mate: the moving origin's Z, X and Y are lined up with the fixed origin's. isFlipped adds the half turn. The fix is to swap the two branches (`if flip { from_rotation_x(PI) } else { IDENTITY }`), or to invert `flip` where the `joint` command is parsed in crates/engine/src/mates.rs.

None of the existing reference cases hit this path. The ones that use Fusion's Joint API (298–311 and 315–317) all use as-built joints, which return early before the mate. 296–297 and 312–314 use assembly constraints (Constrain Components / Align) and also run through the `joint` command. They depend on the opposite (face-to-face) default and use isFlipped as written now. If Fox maps those to `joint`, keep that behaviour on their path, e.g. as a separate default, rather than changing it for all joints.

I checked these Fusion conventions directly. A planar face's joint Z is its outward normal, and its X is the world X projected onto the face. A vertex origin from createByPoint uses the component's +Z and +X. Offset runs along the fixed origin's Z. Driven rotation is counter-clockwise about the fixed Z, which Fox already does. Two things are still unchecked because the boxes in these cases are symmetric: whether isFlipped turns about X or Y, and how `angle` combines with flip. A follow-up case with an off-centre origin should pin those down.

history.note: I tested Fusion's Pipe along a line, tangent R20 arc, line path on the XZ plane. Fox's `pipe` matches Fusion exactly for a solid round pipe (d=6) and a hollow one (1 mm wall). Fox has no section type and no partial-path distance, and it silently ignores those keys, so it builds a round full-length pipe instead. The square-section case comes out 21% too small with 5 faces instead of 10. The triangular case cut at distance one 0.6 comes out 127% too big, with the wrong bounding box and 5 faces instead of 7. probe.summary: I tested Fusion's Pipe along a line, tangent R20 arc, line path on the XZ plane. Fox's `pipe` matches Fusion exactly for a solid round pipe (d=6) and a hollow one (1 mm wall). Fox has no section type and no partial-path distance, and it silently ignores those keys, so it builds a round full-length pipe instead. probe.fix_hint: In Fox, `pipe` (crates/engine/src/features.rs, the "pipe" arm, plus FeatureKind::Pipe in crates/model/src/lib.rs) only takes diameter and wall. Its regen in crates/model/src/regen/extra.rs always sweeps a circle of radius diameter/2. The fix needs to add three things. (1) A `section` parameter: circular, square or triangular. The size is the diameter, the square's side, or the equilateral triangle's side. Square: a centred 6x6 square at size 6 gives Fusion's numbers exactly (volume 36 x path length). Triangle: in Fusion's triangle the vertex is 2√3 from the path on the -X side at the start, and the centroid sits 1 mm off the path toward -Y (world). Use the triangular-partial-path expected.json to work out the exact placement. The hollow wall applies to every section as an inward offset. (2) `distance_one` and `distance_two` (fractions 0..1 of the path length from each end) to trim the path before sweeping. (3) Reject unknown keys, or at least `section` and `distance`, instead of silently building a round full-length pipe. In the Fox scripts I used the keys "section" and "distance". To test this in Fusion I added op_pipe to tools/fusion-bridge/FoxBridge/recipe_runner.py; its recipe keys are section, size, wall, distance_one and distance_two.

fix.summary:
Fox's `pipe` could only sweep a circle along the whole path. It also silently ignored `section` and `distance`, so square and partial pipes came out as round full-length ones. The 4 Fusion cases (84 to 87) now match expected.json and are added to baseline.txt.

**Changes**
- **Model:** `FeatureKind::Pipe` has two new fields, both serde-defaulted so older .fox files still load:
  - `section`: a new `PipeSection` enum with circular, square and triangular.
  - `distance`: the fraction of the path to follow, measured from its start. `for_each_expr` visits it.
- **Section shapes** (in `regen/extra.rs`):
  - The section plane's x runs across the path in the sketch plane and its y along the sketch normal.
  - Square: a centred square whose side is the size.
  - Triangular: an equilateral triangle whose *height* is the size, so its side is 2/√3 × size. The base is centred on the path at −size/2 along the sketch normal and the apex is at +size/2, so the centroid sits size/6 below the path. I worked this out from the answer key: the area is 12√3 for size 6, the Y range is ±3, the centroid y is −1 and the X range is ±2√3.
  - The wall is an inward offset for every section shape.
  - Square and triangular pipes are run through `unified()` so each flat side is one face along its straight runs, as in Fusion (10 and 7 faces).
- **Partial path:** before sweeping, the path is cut to its first `distance` × length. This is exact for lines and arcs. Splines and ellipse arcs are measured by sampling; spline pieces are split at the cut (de Casteljau) and ellipse arcs shortened.
- **Command:** `pipe` takes `section` (circular, square or triangular), `size` as another name for `diameter`, and `distance` or `distance_one`. It now rejects keys it doesn't know and unknown section names. The help text is updated.
- **UI:** the Pipe form has new Section and Distance inputs.
- **Tests and docs:** a new engine test, `pipe_sections_and_partial_paths`, checks volumes, the triangle's placement, half of a spline path, and the rejection of unknown keys. The README line on pipes is updated.

**Checks**
- `reference_parts` passes, all four new cases included.
- The fox-model, fox-engine and fox-ui tests pass, except `fuzz_found_bugs` in `crates/engine/tests/fuzz_features.rs`. It fails on seed 1022 with "Body1 is not a valid solid" after chamfer and cut steps. That test never calls pipe and nothing it runs uses the changed code, but I didn't run it on main to confirm it was failing before.
- `cargo fmt` is clean.
- Clippy is clean on fox-model, fox-engine and fox-ui only after allowing one new lint (`chunks_exact_to_as_chunks`). The local toolchain is Rust 1.99, while CI pins 1.97 (which isn't installed here), and that lint fires on existing fox-exchange code.

**Limits**
- `distance_two` isn't supported: the command rejects it rather than guessing what it means.
- The triangle's apex direction (toward the sketch normal) comes from this one Fusion case only.

(2) Multi-face skins: each face is thickened separately and the slabs are unioned, which leaves a notch at convex edges between faces (L case: 2475 vs 2500 mm³ at ±1, 10 vs 8 faces). Fox's `thicken` now behaves like Fusion's Thicken.

**Symmetric thickness.** The thickness now goes on each side of the surface, so 2 mm gives 4 mm in all, as in Fusion. Before, Fox split the value in half. Case 83 (from SolidCraft, which treats the symmetric value as the total) now uses `thickness: 1` in its part.jsonl, with a comment saying why. `tools/reference-import` halves symmetric thicknesses the same way. Saved `.fox` files that use symmetric thicken will rebuild twice as thick; there is no file migration.

**Multi-face surfaces.** A surface with several faces is now offset as one shell instead of face by face, so the corners where faces meet close up instead of leaving a notch.

history.note: I tested Fusion's Thread against Fox's `thread` command with four cases: a modeled external M10 thread on a rod, a modeled internal M10 thread in a tube bore, a partial left-hand M12 thread with a length and offset, and a cosmetic M8 thread. Fusion built all four and Fox mismatches on every one. Fusion resizes the cylinder to the size and class mean diameter, even for a cosmetic thread (the M8 6g rod becomes Ø7.866). It also cuts a truncated ISO profile and makes few faces (6 on the rod, 7 in the tube). Fox keeps the drawn diameter and cuts a sharp 60° V groove, giving 20 and 18 faces. The volume differences run from -3.9% to +9.1%, and Fox puts the partial-length thread at the other end of the rod. Cases: 92-external-modeled-full, 93-internal-modeled-full, 94-external-modeled-partial-left, 95-external-cosmetic.

probe.summary: I tested Fusion's Thread against Fox's `thread` command with four cases: a modeled external M10 thread on a rod, a modeled internal M10 thread in a tube bore, a partial left-hand M12 thread with a length and offset, and a cosmetic M8 thread. Fusion built all four and Fox mismatches on every one. Fusion resizes the cylinder to the size and class mean diameter, even for a cosmetic thread (the M8 6g rod becomes Ø7.866). It also cuts a truncated ISO profile and makes few faces (6 on the rod, 7 in the tube). Fox keeps the drawn diameter and cuts a sharp 60° V groove, giving 20 and 18 faces. The volume differences run from -3.9% to +9.1%, and Fox puts the partial-length thread at the other end of the rod.
probe.fix_hint:
The gap is in the `FeatureKind::Thread` arm of crates/model/src/regen/extra.rs and in `thread_groove` in the same file. Four changes would close it:

1. **Diameter:** Fox only knows the pitch. It needs thread size and class data, as Fusion's `ThreadInfo` has (the designation, the class and the major, minor and pitch diameters). It should then resize the selected cylinder before threading, for both cosmetic and modeled threads. External threads go to the class-mean major diameter (M10 6g → Ø9.85, M12 6g → Ø11.8335, M8 6g → Ø7.866). Internal threads go to the class-mean minor diameter. Today a cosmetic thread leaves the solid untouched.
2. **Profile:** cut the ISO 68-1 truncated profile between those diameters, with a P/8 flat at the crest and a P/4 flat at the root. Fox now cuts a sharp 60° V with a fixed depth (0.6134P external, 0.5413P internal) measured from the drawn radius.
3. **Start end:** with `length` and `offset` and no flip, Fox measures from the opposite end to Fusion's default low end on a +Z-extruded rod. The centre-of-mass z is 14.79 in Fox and 15.29 in Fusion. The end that `cylinder_extent`'s t0 maps to should match Fusion's LowEnd (the z=0 end here).
4. **Faces:** Fox's `helix_sweep` groove splits into many faces (20 against 6 on the rod, 18 against 7 in the tube). Fusion builds the thread as a single helical face set.

I also added an `op_thread` to tools/fusion-bridge/FoxBridge/recipe_runner.py. It takes `face` or `faces`, `internal`, `thread_type`, `designation`, `class`, `modeled`, `right_handed`, `full_length`, `length`, `offset` and `location` (`low_end` or `high_end`).

fix.summary:
Fox's `thread` command now builds threads the way Fusion's Thread command does. All four new reference cases (92–95) pass and survive the 15% edit check. They are added to `baseline.txt` and `edit-baseline.txt`. `cargo test -p fox-engine --test reference_parts` passes with no regressions.

**What changed**
- **Size and class (diameter):**
  - `thread` now takes an ISO metric `designation` (`M10x1.5`, or `M10` for the coarse pitch) and a `class` (default `6g` outside, `6H` inside). It also accepts Fusion-style `location: low_end|high_end` and `right_handed`.
  - The selected cylinder is resized to the class-mean diameter for cosmetic and modeled threads alike: the major diameter outside, the minor diameter inside. For example, M8 6g gives Ø7.866 and M10 6H gives a Ø8.526 bore.
  - The diameters come from the ISO 965-1 deviation and tolerance tables in a new `fox_model::thread` module.
  - Without a designation, the drawn diameter is taken as the basic size and the solid is not resized, so older designs keep their size.
- **Profile:** a modeled thread cuts the ISO 68-1 profile: 60° flanks half a pitch apart at the class-mean pitch diameter, with a flat root.
  - I fitted the root diameter from Fusion's measured volume and area: outside, the mean of d1 max and d3 min; inside, the mean of D and D2 max + 11H/12.
  - The same fit reproduced the class-mean pitch diameters (8.928 and 9.116) to within about 0.0002.
- **Thread ends:** the groove is swept a pitch past each end, then cut off by planes square to the axis at the thread's ends. Fusion's partial-thread area and face count only match this.
- **Start end:** `length` and `offset` now count from the face's low end along a fixed axis direction, matching Fusion's LowEnd.
- **Face count:** a helical cut leaves the crest cylinder as one strip per turn.
  - A new kernel step, `merge_cylinder_strips` (`cpp/threads.cpp`), joins the strips into one face. This gives Fusion's counts: 6 faces on the rod, 7 in the tube, 8 on the partial thread.
  - OCCT's standard integration is inaccurate on a face that wraps more than one turn. For such shapes, `mass_props` now measures volume against a plane square to the axis, where the crest contributes nothing. Other shapes are measured exactly as before.
- **Bore picking bug:** `FaceRef::resolve` now also scores curved faces by distance to the surface. A tube's bore and outer wall share a centroid, so picking the bore used to resolve to the outer cylinder.
- **Scripts:** the four `part.jsonl` scripts now pass the recipe's designation and class instead of only a pitch.
- **Tests:** the thread form gained size and class fields. New tests cover the ISO class means, the strip merge in the kernel, and engine threads by size and class.

**Test status**
- `cargo fmt` is clean.
- Clippy is clean on the changed crates. The local toolchain (1.99, newer than CI's pinned 1.97) flags a new `chunks_exact_to_as_chunks` lint, but only in crates this PR doesn't touch.
- `fuzz_found_bugs` (seed 1022, no threads involved) fails, and fails the same way on unmodified HEAD.

Contour Flange constructs multiple bends and faces based on open sketch profile.

tooltip:
Bends the sheet metal model along the selected sketch lines with one face fixed.

Angle, position, and relief options control how the sheet metal is folded.

name: Hem
tooltip:
Folds sheet metal edge back onto itself.

You can create the following hems: Open, Flat, Double, Rolled, Teardrop, and Rope.

name: Lofted Flange
tooltip:
Creates a sheet metal flange that transitions between two sketch profiles.

Commonly used in duct fabrication.

name: Corner Closure
tooltip: Adjusts the gap and relief shape of a corner that is formed by two flanges.

name: Join by bend
tooltip:
Joins two separate sheet metal bodies by creating a connecting bend.

Material may be added to one or both bodies to connect them.

name: Rip
tooltip:
Creates a Rip on a sheet metal flange along an edge, between two points, or removes a face.

Select a face to remove, an edge to rip along, or two points to define the start and end of the rip. If selecting two points or an edge, specify the Gap Width value.

name: Sheet Metal Chamfer
tooltip:
Bevels thickness edges of sheet metal flanges by a specified distance.

Chamfers remove sharp corners to improve safety, reduce edge stress, and help sheet metal parts fit and assemble more easily with other components.

name: Sheet Metal Fillet
tooltip:
Rounds thickness edges of sheet metal flanges by a specified radius.

Fillets remove sharp corners and can help distribute stress at corners, and improve coating or finishing by allowing more uniform coverage along edges.

name: Sheet Metal Rules
tooltip:
Rules control the thickness, bend radius, reliefs, and other settings related to sheet metal design.

Create and edit rules in the active document to change your designs. Save rules to the library to make them accessible in other designs.

name: Sheet Metal Rules Library
tooltip:
Manage and reuse sheet metal rules across designs.

Create, edit, and save rules in the library to make them accessible in other designs.

name: Unfold
tooltip:
Flattens selected bends with one face fixed so you can add features across flanges.

Any changes made in the flat state remain in the folded model.

name: Refold
tooltip:
Returns the model to its folded shape.

Any changes made in the flat state remain in the folded model.

name: Box
tooltip:
Creates a surface body box.

Select a plane, draw a rectangle then specify the height of the box.
paths: Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Create

name: Coil
tooltip:
Creates a surface coil.

Select a plane then draw a circle to specify the major diameter of the coil. Finish defining the coil using the manipulators or dialog box.
paths: Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Create

name: Cylinder
tooltip:
Creates a surface body cylinder.

Select a plane, draw a circle then specify the height of the cylinder.
paths: Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Create

name: Extrude
tooltip:
Adds depth to open or closed sketch profiles or planar faces.

Select the profile or planar face then specify the distance to extrude.
paths: Edit Model > EDIT MODEL SURFACE > Create
Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Create

name: Loft
tooltip:
Creates a smooth shape that transitions between two or more sketch profiles or faces.

Select a series of profiles, planar faces, or non-planar faces to define the shape. Optionally, select rails or centerlines to guide the shape.
paths: Edit Model > EDIT MODEL SURFACE > Create
Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Create

name: Offset
tooltip:
Creates a new surface body at a given distance from the selected face or surface body.

Select a face or surface body to offset, then specify the distance.
paths: Edit Model > EDIT MODEL SURFACE > Create
Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Create

name: Patch
tooltip:
Creates a planar or 3D surface within the boundary of a specified closed loop.

Select the loop to patch then apply connected (G0), tangent (G1), and curvature (G2) boundary conditions.
paths: Edit Model > EDIT MODEL SURFACE > Create
Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Create

name: Pipe
tooltip:
Creates a surface pipe that follows a selected path.

Select the path then specify the section and size.
paths: Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Create

name: Revolve
tooltip:
Revolves a sketch profile or planar face around a selected axis.

Select a profile or planar face and an axis to revolve around, then specify the extent type, direction, and operation.
paths: Edit Model > EDIT MODEL SURFACE > Create
Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Create

name: Ruled
tooltip:
Creates a ruled surface at a specified distance and angle from selected edges.

Select edges on a solid body, surface body, or sketch. Then select a ruled surface type and specify the direction, distance, and angle.
paths: Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Create

name: Sphere
tooltip:
Creates a surface sphere.

Select a plane then specify the center point of the sphere and the diameter.
paths: Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Create

name: Sweep
tooltip:
Sweeps a sketch profile or planar face along a selected path.

Select the profile then select the sweep path. The distance for the sweep is a decimal percentage of the selected path.
paths: Edit Model > EDIT MODEL SURFACE > Create
Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Create

name: Torus
tooltip:
Creates a surface torus.

Specify the center point and diameter of the axis of revolution of the torus.
paths: Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Create

name: Extend
tooltip:
Enlarges a surface by extending its edges a specified distance.

Select the edges of a surface, select an extension type, then specify the distance to extend. Select an edge alignment option to control the curvature continuity between faces.
paths: Edit Model > EDIT MODEL SURFACE > Modify
Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Modify

name: Merge
tooltip:
Combines the selected faces into a single quilt surface.

Select the faces to merge. You can select solid or surface faces.
paths: Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Modify

name: Reverse Normal
tooltip:
Flips the positive direction of all faces on a selected surface body.

Select a surface body to reverse.
paths: Edit Model > EDIT MODEL SURFACE > Modify
Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Modify

name: Stitch
tooltip:
Joins surfaces to make a single surface body or solid body.

Select the surfaces to join. Edges within the tolerance are highlighted green.
paths: Edit Model > EDIT MODEL SURFACE > Modify
Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Modify

name: Trim
tooltip:
Removes the selected area of a surface body using the specified cutting tool.

Select the cutting tool to use then select faces or surface bodies to remove.
paths: Edit Model > EDIT MODEL SURFACE > Modify
Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Modify

name: Unstitch
tooltip:
Breaks joined surfaces into individual surfaces.

Select faces to unstitch. The selected face is unhooked from the parent body and the result body contains the unhooked face.
paths: Edit Model > EDIT MODEL SURFACE > Modify
Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Modify

name: Untrim
tooltip:
Extends trimmed surfaces and fills gaps, holes, or empty regions.

Select the surface to untrim, then select the untrim type. You can untrim all edges, internal edges, external edges, or manually select the edges you want to untrim.
paths: Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Modify

name: Bill of Materials
tooltip:
Opens the bill of materials for this design.

(May not be available in some situations, such as when viewing a configured design, or when Fusion is offline.)

name: Scripts and Add-Ins...
tooltip:
Manage Scripts and Add-Ins

Displays the Scripts and Add-Ins dialog box. Create, edit, run, stop, debug and manage Scripts and Add-Ins.

name: Geometric Tolerancing
tooltip:
Creates a product manufacturing information (PMI) geometric tolerance annotation.

Add geometric tolerancing feature control frames and datum icons to annotate geometric tolerances on model geometry.

name: Hole/Thread Note
tooltip:
Creates a product manufacturing information (PMI) note for a hole or boss, with or without threads.

Add a leader line and include units, diameter, depth, thread information, tolerance, and text. The information stays with the feature and can be reused in downstream manufacturing workflows, such as automated hole drilling.

name: Note
tooltip:
Creates a product manufacturing information (PMI) general note.

Add a leader line and include general information, such as instructions, references to standards, or clarifications.

name: Sizes and Dimensions
tooltip:
Creates a product manufacturing information (PMI) for dimensions.

Add linear, angular, radius, or diameter dimensions to the model.

name: 3D Print
tooltip:
Prepares solid or mesh bodies to be 3D printed directly from Fusion's Manufacture workspace or from an external application.

Select solid or mesh bodies to prepare, then select a Preparation Type to switch to the Manufacture workspace, export and send to an installed 3D printing application, or export a 3MF, STL, or OBJ file. For exports, adjust the output and refinement settings to control the resolution of the mesh.
paths: Sheet Metal > Direct Mesh Editing > Export

name: Finish Base Feature
tooltip: Return to the Design workspace.
where: Design > BASE FEATURE SOLID > Finish Base Feature
paths: Form > BASE FEATURE SOLID > Finish Base Feature

Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SOLID > Finish Base Feature
Sheet Metal > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Finish Base Feature

PCB > BASE FEATURE SURFACE > Finish Base Feature
